title: Thyroid nodule / neck swelling
scenario: Picture of a lady with a solitary thyroid nodule (discussion station). 430A
Picture of an anterior neck swelling. Old exam
A woman in her 40s with a hyperfunctioning (toxic) solitary thyroid nodule. Archive
Neck-lump history: papillary thyroid cancer (on thyroxine). 436A
Neck mass with a family history. 441F

imgs.cap: Solitary thyroid nodule (430A) Anterior neck swelling (similar to the exam picture)

qs.q: Take a history from the patient (focus on the thyroid).
a: Lump: when/how noticed, painful?, change in size, disappears?, other lumps, discharge. Local effects: dysphagia, dyspnoea, voice change.
Function: hyper- and hypothyroid symptoms, system by system.
Risk factors: radiation exposure, family history of thyroid cancer / MEN, previous neck surgery; PMH (cancer, pregnancy, recent infection); iodine-containing drugs.
qs.why: Characterise the lump, its local pressure effects, the thyroid status, and the risk factors for cancer (radiation, family history, MEN).
hist: Lump: when and how noticed, painful, change in size
Sudden painful enlargement suggests haemorrhage into a nodule; steady growth raises suspicion of cancer.
Disappears? Other lumps, discharge
Help separate a thyroid nodule from other neck swellings (cysts, nodes).
Dysphagia, dyspnoea, voice change
Local compression or invasion; voice change suggests recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement by cancer.
Hyper- and hypothyroid symptoms
Thyroid function guides investigation (a hot nodule is rarely malignant).
Radiation exposure
The main environmental risk factor for papillary cancer.
Family history of thyroid cancer / MEN
Familial and medullary thyroid cancer.
PMH (cancer, pregnancy, recent infection), iodine drugs
Recent viral illness → subacute thyroiditis; pregnancy affects function and timing.

qs.q: Examine the neck.
a: Inspect (swallow & tongue protrusion), palpate from behind (size, consistency, nodules, tenderness, mobility), trachea, lymph nodes, percuss for retrosternal extension, auscultate for bruit; thyroid status (pulse, tremor, eyes, reflexes).
qs.why: Inspection with swallowing and tongue protrusion separates thyroid from thyroglossal swellings; palpation from behind, lymph nodes and thyroid status complete it.

qs.q: What is your differential diagnosis?
a: Solitary nodule: cyst, adenoma, malignancy (papillary, follicular…), dominant nodule of MNG, toxic nodule.
Unilateral neck swelling: + thyroglossal cyst, branchial cyst, lymph node.
qs.why: A solitary nodule may be a cyst, adenoma, dominant nodule of MNG or cancer; other neck swellings (thyroglossal, branchial cyst, nodes) are included if the lump isn't thyroid.

qs.q: How can you tell benign from malignant from the history? Is this nodule benign or malignant, and why?
a: A hyperfunctioning (hot) nodule is usually benign — malignant cells don't take up iodine.
qs.why: A hot nodule traps iodine — malignant cells rarely do — so autonomously functioning nodules are almost always benign.

qs.q: What investigations will you order?
a: Baseline: CBC, U&E, ECG. Thyroid function: TSH and free T4.
US (cystic vs solid, features) → FNA (Bethesda: benign, malignant, non-diagnostic,
suspicious/follicular).
Hyperthyroid → radionuclide scan (hot vs cold). Calcitonin if medullary is suspected (only thyroid cancer with a marker); TSI.
qs.why: TFTs first; US characterises the nodule and FNA (Bethesda) is the key test for malignancy; a scan is used if hyperthyroid; calcitonin if medullary is suspected.

qs.q: What is the management?
a: Toxic solitary nodule: antithyroid drug to control (e.g. PTU), then radioactive iodine; if it fails/contraindicated → surgery (lobectomy).
Malignancy: thyroidectomy (total or lobectomy by size/risk) ± central neck dissection, ± RAI ablation, TSH-suppressive thyroxine.
qs.why: A toxic nodule is controlled medically then ablated by RAI or removed; cancer is treated by thyroidectomy, ± RAI ablation and TSH suppression.

qs.q: What are the indications for radioactive iodine?
a: (After thyroidectomy for cancer) nodal or distant metastasis, extrathyroidal extension, tumour > 1 cm / bilateral disease; also toxic nodules / Graves.
qs.why: After thyroidectomy for differentiated cancer, RAI ablates remnant/metastatic tissue in higher-risk disease; RAI is also a treatment for toxic nodules/Graves.

qs.q: What are the contraindications to radioactive iodine?
a: Pregnancy & breastfeeding, children, previous radiation therapy.
qs.why: Radiation crosses the placenta and into breast milk and harms the developing thyroid — pregnancy and breastfeeding are absolute contraindications.

qs.q: What are the indications for thyroidectomy?
a: Suspected or proven malignancy, thyrotoxicosis (failed/contraindicated other therapy), compression of trachea/oesophagus, cosmetic.
qs.why: Surgery is for cancer (or suspicion), compression, thyrotoxicosis not suited to other treatment, and cosmesis.

qs.q: What are the complications of thyroidectomy?
a: Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, transient hypoparathyroidism / hypocalcaemia (parathyroid ischaemia), hypothyroidism, haematoma.
qs.why: Nerve injury, hypocalcaemia from parathyroid ischaemia, bleeding and hypothyroidism are the classic complications.

qs.q: How do you follow up the patient?
a: Differentiated (papillary) cancer: lifelong thyroxine (TSH suppression), serum thyroglobulin + anti-Tg antibodies, neck US ± radioiodine whole-body scan.
Medullary: calcitonin & CEA, US.
qs.why: Thyroglobulin is made only by thyroid tissue — after total thyroidectomy + RAI it should be undetectable, so a rise signals recurrence; calcitonin/CEA do the same for medullary cancer.

a: Features: diffuse hyperaemic goitre with bruit, exophthalmos, pretibial myxoedema, young/middle-aged; TSI positive.
Treatment: antithyroid drugs (PTU/methimazole) → radioactive iodine if failure, non-compliance or agranulocytosis → subtotal/total thyroidectomy when RAI isn't possible (pregnancy, children).
Commonest cause of hyperthyroidism: Graves'; of hypothyroidism: Hashimoto's.

extra.q: Extra case — Medullary thyroid cancer (20-year-old, FNA consistent with MTC)
a: Associated syndrome: MEN 2 (MTC, phaeochromocytoma, parathyroid hyperplasia).
Next step: look for phaeochromocytoma (plasma/urine metanephrines).
If positive: remove the phaeochromocytoma first (phenoxybenzamine ~14 days, β-blocker 2 days pre-op), then total thyroidectomy + central neck dissection within ~2 weeks (not together).
Follow-up: history, exam, US, calcitonin.

title: Multinodular goitre
scenario: Picture of a multinodular goitre. Archive
A patient with an anterior neck swelling gradually increasing in size. (counted as new in 442F) 442F

imgs.cap: Multinodular goitre Large anterior neck swelling (442F)

qs.q: What is the diagnosis?
a: Multinodular goitre.
qs.why: A diffusely enlarged thyroid with multiple nodules is a multinodular goitre.

qs.q: What is your differential diagnosis?
a: Multinodular goitre, thyroid malignancy.
qs.why: A dominant or growing nodule in a goitre may be malignant, so cancer is the key differential.

qs.q: What are the important questions to ask in the history?
a: Lump: onset, how noticed, progression, pain, discharge, redness.
Function: hyper/hypothyroid symptoms (heat intolerance, palpitations, tremor,
diarrhoea/constipation, menstrual change, mood, weight change).
Compression: pressure, SOB/stridor, voice change, dysphagia.
Other swellings, constitutional symptoms; risk factors: family history of thyroid cancer, MEN, radiation; PMH; iodine-containing drugs; previous neck surgery/radiotherapy.
qs.why: The history assesses three things: the lump, thyroid function (hyper/hypo), and compression (airway, oesophagus, recurrent laryngeal nerve), plus cancer risk factors.
hist: Lump: onset, how noticed, progression
Rapid growth suggests malignancy or haemorrhage into a nodule.
Pain, discharge, redness
Suggest thyroiditis or infection.
Hyperthyroid symptoms (heat intolerance, palpitations, tremor, diarrhoea, weight loss)
Assess function — a toxic multinodular goitre needs control before surgery.
Hypothyroid symptoms (cold intolerance, constipation, weight gain, menstrual change, mood)
The other side of the function assessment.
Pressure, SOB/stridor
Tracheal compression, especially with retrosternal extension.
Voice change
Recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement — suggests malignancy.
Dysphagia
Oesophageal compression.
Other swellings, constitutional symptoms
Lymph nodes and weight loss suggest cancer.
Family history of thyroid cancer, MEN, radiation
Risk factors for thyroid cancer (radiation → papillary; MEN → medullary).
Iodine-containing drugs, previous neck surgery/radiotherapy
Iodine and amiodarone affect thyroid function; previous surgery affects operative planning.

qs.q: What are the findings on examination?
a: Diffusely enlarged thyroid with an irregular nodular surface, moves with swallowing, usually non-tender, may have tracheal deviation; check for cervical lymphadenopathy (and retrosternal extension, Pemberton's).
qs.why: Thyroid swellings move with swallowing (attached to the larynx by pretracheal fascia); a goitre is nodular, may deviate the trachea or extend retrosternally.

qs.q: How would you investigate?
a: TSH (+ T4), thyroid ultrasound, FNA of dominant/suspicious nodules (442F doctor wanted to hear FNA immediately).
Normal/hypo → US then FNA; hyper → radionuclide scan. Calcitonin (medullary), TSI; baseline CBC, U&E, ECG.
qs.why: TSH decides the pathway (scan only if hyperthyroid); ultrasound characterises nodules; FNA of dominant/suspicious nodules excludes cancer.

qs.q: What is the management?
a: Stable, asymptomatic → observation and follow-up.
Toxic MNG → β-blocker + definitive treatment (radioiodine or surgery).
Compressive symptoms / suspicious nodule → surgery (thyroidectomy) — what the doctor wanted to hear.
qs.why: A benign, euthyroid, asymptomatic goitre can be watched; toxicity, compression or a suspicious nodule are indications for surgery (or RAI for toxic goitre).

qs.q: What are the complications of thyroid surgery?
a: Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury (hoarseness), superior laryngeal nerve injury, hypocalcaemia (parathyroid injury — tingling, tetany), neck haematoma (airway obstruction), hypothyroidism.
qs.why: The structures at risk are the recurrent and superior laryngeal nerves, the parathyroids (hypocalcaemia) and the vessels (haematoma); removing the gland causes hypothyroidism.

qs.q: If one recurrent laryngeal nerve is injured, what happens? If both?
a: One → hoarseness (dysphonia). Both → airway obstruction / stridor — life-threatening (may need tracheostomy).
qs.why: One RLN palsy paralyses one vocal cord (hoarse voice); both leave the cords near the midline — airway obstruction needing intubation/tracheostomy.

qs.q: Post-op day 1 the patient is desaturating with difficulty breathing — what do you suspect and what will you do?
a: Neck haematoma compressing the airway → emergency: open the wound at the bedside (remove sutures/clips) to evacuate the haematoma, then urgent transfer to the OR.
qs.why: A haematoma in the closed neck compresses the airway — release it at the bedside immediately (open the wound) before returning to theatre.

qs.q: What do you look for after surgery?
a: Voice changes, signs of hypocalcaemia, neck swelling/respiratory distress.
qs.why: Post-thyroidectomy checks target the three early dangers: nerve injury (voice), parathyroid injury (calcium) and bleeding (neck swelling, breathing).

qs.q: How do you manage these complications?
a: Hypocalcaemia → IV calcium gluconate, then oral calcium + vitamin D.
Haematoma → immediate decompression + surgery.
RLN injury → ENT assessment & follow-up.
qs.why: Each complication has a specific fix: calcium (IV then oral + vitamin D), haematoma decompression, ENT assessment of the cords.

qs.q: What are the earliest symptoms of hypocalcaemia?
a: Numbness/tingling of the fingers and around the mouth, muscle cramps; then tetany/carpopedal spasm, laryngospasm/stridor, convulsions, arrhythmias ("CATs go numb").
qs.why: Low calcium raises nerve excitability — perioral and fingertip tingling come first, then cramps, carpopedal spasm and tetany.

extra.q: Complications of a long-standing goitre; tests and management of hypocalcaemia
a: Complications: toxic (hot) nodule / toxic MNG, malignancy, calcification, haemorrhage/degeneration. Early hypocalcaemia tests: Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs.
Treatment: Ca > 2 mmol/L → oral calcium carbonate 600 mg BD; < 2 → add vitamin D; very low, carpopedal spasm or stridor → slow IV 10 % calcium gluconate.

qs.q: Examine the thyroid (thyroid status).
a: Introduce, consent, position sitting with neck exposed.
Inspect: swelling, scars; ask to swallow water and protrude the tongue.
Palpate from behind (each lobe & isthmus, while swallowing) — size, shape, consistency, nodules, tenderness; trachea; cervical lymph nodes.
Percuss the manubrium (retrosternal extension); auscultate each lobe for a bruit.
Thyroid status: hands (tremor, sweating, palmar erythema), pulse, eyes (exophthalmos, lid lag), reflexes, proximal myopathy, pretibial myxoedema.
qs.why: A systematic examination covers the gland (inspection, palpation from behind with swallowing, retrosternal percussion, bruit) and the patient's thyroid status (hands, pulse, eyes, reflexes).

qs.q: What is the diagnosis?
a: Primary hyperparathyroidism.
qs.why: Raised calcium with raised or inappropriately normal PTH = primary hyperparathyroidism, usually a single adenoma.

qs.q: Take a focused history.
a: "Stones, bones, groans, moans": renal stones/polyuria, bone pain/fractures, abdominal pain/constipation/pancreatitis/PUD, depression/fatigue/confusion; drugs (thiazides, lithium), family history (MEN).
qs.why: Hypercalcaemia affects kidneys (stones, polyuria), bones, gut (constipation, pancreatitis, PUD) and mind — "stones, bones, groans, moans".
hist: Renal stones, polyuria ("stones")
High calcium is excreted in the urine → stones and polyuria.
Bone pain, fractures ("bones")
PTH releases calcium from bone → osteoporosis and osteitis fibrosa cystica.
Abdominal pain, constipation, pancreatitis, PUD ("groans")
Hypercalcaemia reduces gut motility and stimulates gastrin and pancreatic enzymes.
Depression, fatigue, confusion ("moans")
Neuropsychiatric effects of hypercalcaemia.
Thiazides, lithium
Drugs that raise calcium and must be excluded.
Family history (MEN)
Hyperparathyroidism is part of MEN 1 and MEN 2A — affects the surgical plan.

qs.q: What investigations?
a: Labs: serum calcium (high), phosphate (low), PTH (high), vitamin D, U&E/creatinine, 24-h urine calcium.
Imaging: sestamibi (nuclear) scan + neck US to localise; DEXA scan.
qs.why: Biochemistry confirms the diagnosis (and 24-h urine calcium excludes FHH); sestamibi + US localise the adenoma for focused surgery; DEXA measures bone damage.

qs.q: What is the treatment?
a: Surgical excision of the adenoma (parathyroidectomy).
qs.why: Removing the adenoma cures the disease.

notes.t: The 437 file also lists "Primary parathyroid" as a case, but no questions were written down.

title: Phaeochromocytoma / adrenal mass
scenario: A 32-year-old with refractory hypertension despite multiple medications. 439F

qs.q: What will you ask in the history?
a: Hypertension: new? controlled?; episodic headache, palpitations, sweating, panic attacks; chronic diarrhoea; episodes?
PMH of cancer; family history of adrenal tumours or MEN syndrome.
qs.why: Refractory hypertension in a young patient suggests a secondary cause; paroxysms of headache, palpitations and sweating point to phaeochromocytoma, and family history to MEN2/VHL.
hist: Hypertension: new, controlled
New, resistant or paroxysmal hypertension suggests a secondary cause such as phaeochromocytoma.
Episodic headache, palpitations, sweating
The classic triad of catecholamine surges.
Panic attacks, episodes
Paroxysmal attacks are typical of phaeochromocytoma.
Chronic diarrhoea
May reflect catecholamine or associated hormone secretion.
PMH of cancer
An adrenal mass may be a metastasis.
Family history of adrenal tumours or MEN
Phaeochromocytoma occurs in MEN 2, VHL and NF1.

qs.q: What will you look for on physical examination?
a: General appearance, vitals (↑BP, ↑HR), Cushingoid features (moon face, buffalo hump, striae, acne, hirsutism, bruising, central obesity); a large mass may be palpable.
qs.why: Examination looks for the signs of the other adrenal causes (Cushing's) and for complications of hypertension.

qs.q: What labs will you ask for?
a: CBC, coagulation; plasma free / 24-h urine metanephrines (phaeo), VMA.
Electrolytes (↑Na, ↓K suggests Conn's) + aldosterone : renin ratio (> 30–40 = Conn's). 24-h urine free cortisol (Cushing's).
qs.why: Each functional adrenal tumour has its screening test: metanephrines (phaeo), aldosterone/renin ratio with hypokalaemia (Conn's), urinary cortisol (Cushing's).

qs.q: What imaging will you ask for?
a: CT adrenal protocol (± MRI, US), ECG.
qs.why: Biochemistry first, then an adrenal-protocol CT localises the tumour.

qs.q: Describe what you see.
a: Coronal CT abdomen showing a mass in the left adrenal gland.
qs.why: Name the modality and side: a coronal CT showing a left adrenal mass.

qs.q: What is your differential diagnosis? (4)
a: Phaeochromocytoma, incidentaloma (non-functioning adenoma), Cushing's (cortisol-secreting adenoma), (myelo)lipoma.
Others: Conn's adenoma, adrenocortical carcinoma, metastasis.
qs.why: An adrenal mass is either functional (phaeo, Cushing's, Conn's) or non-functional (incidentaloma, myelolipoma), or malignant (carcinoma, metastasis).

qs.q: What is the clinical presentation?
a: Hyperthyroid symptoms + exophthalmos, pretibial myxoedema, thyroid acropachy; diffuse, smooth, vascular goitre (bruit) in young/middle-aged women.
qs.why: TSH-receptor antibodies stimulate the whole gland (diffuse vascular goitre, thyrotoxicosis) and cause the autoimmune extrathyroidal signs — eye disease and pretibial myxoedema are specific to Graves'.

qs.q: What investigations?
a: TFT (↓TSH, ↑T4/T3), TSH-receptor antibodies (thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin), US (diffuse, hypervascular), radionuclide scan (diffuse increased uptake).
qs.why: TFTs confirm hyperthyroidism and the antibodies prove the cause; a scan shows diffuse uptake (vs a hot nodule or thyroiditis with low uptake).

qs.q: What is the management?
a: 1st: antithyroid drugs (carbimazole/methimazole; PTU in 1st-trimester pregnancy) + β-blocker. 2nd: radioactive iodine (failure, non-compliance, side effects such as agranulocytosis). 3rd: total thyroidectomy when RAI isn't possible (pregnancy, children, severe eye disease, large goitre).
qs.why: β-blockers control symptoms and antithyroid drugs block hormone synthesis; RAI or surgery give a definitive cure. RAI can worsen eye disease and is contraindicated in pregnancy — then surgery.

qs.q: Commonest cause of hypothyroidism and of hyperthyroidism?
a: Hashimoto's thyroiditis (iodine deficiency worldwide) / Graves' disease.
qs.why: Both are autoimmune: Hashimoto's antibodies destroy the gland; Graves' antibodies stimulate it.

title: Medullary thyroid cancer & MEN2
scenario: A 20-year-old woman with a neck swelling. FNA: consistent with medullary thyroid cancer.

qs.q: What is the associated syndrome?
a: MEN 2 (RET proto-oncogene). MEN 2A: MTC + phaeochromocytoma + primary hyperparathyroidism. MEN 2B: MTC + phaeo + mucosal neuromas + marfanoid habitus.
qs.why: Medullary carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells; about a quarter are hereditary, as part of MEN2 from RET mutations — especially in a young patient.

qs.q: What is the next step?
a: Exclude phaeochromocytoma: plasma/24-h urine metanephrines (+ calcitonin, CEA, calcium/PTH, RET testing, neck US).
qs.why: An undiagnosed phaeochromocytoma can cause a fatal hypertensive crisis under anaesthesia — it must be excluded before thyroid surgery.

qs.q: Phaeochromocytoma is positive — what do you do?
a: Resect the phaeochromocytoma first after α-blockade (phenoxybenzamine ≈ 10–14 days) then β-blocker (≈ 2–3 days pre-op); then total thyroidectomy + central neck dissection later.
qs.why: The phaeo is the immediate danger, so it is removed first; α-blockade before β-blockade prevents unopposed α-vasoconstriction (crisis).

qs.q: How do you follow up?
a: History, examination, neck US, serum calcitonin and CEA.
qs.why: Calcitonin and CEA are secreted by C-cell tumours, so rising levels signal recurrence.
